turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning. Come on through, both of you, and have a seat. What can I do for you today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Bit of a waste of your time, if I'm honest. It's just the toe.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Just the toe, he says. He was awake half the—
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I was not awake half the night. I dozed. Right big toe's a bit swollen, that's all. Came on yesterday afternoon.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yesterday afternoon, was it?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, scratch that. I was fine in the afternoon. It was last night, once I got into bed. Started throbbing then.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): And if you had to put a word to it?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): A niggle. Three out of ten, if you want a number. I walked in, didn't I?
[SEG0009] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He couldn't get his trainer on this morning. He was hanging off the kitchen doorframe, so don't let him—
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. It kept me up. There, I've said it. Still hardly an emergency.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which foot?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. The big toe. Left one's got nothing to do with it.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): When you look at it, is it red, or hot?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Hot, a bit, yeah. I haven't studied it. She says it's red.
[SEG0015] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Bright red and shiny, right over the joint. You can see it from the doorway.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chance you injured it? Stubbed it, kicked something?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. I haven't done anything to it.
[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The chair in the—

[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, yeah, I know. Dining chair, last night, in the hall. I did kick it, I'd forgotten. Mind you, the toe was already going before that... no, I've got it backwards. The kick was first, then it swelled up in bed.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has the same thing ever happened before?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I was going to say no, but there was that time...
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): A year back. Same big toe. Went down in a few days on its own, so I didn't bother coming in.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about medicines? Anything you take regularly, even if it doesn't feel related?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. I'm not one for pills. There's only the...
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Water tablet. Bendroflumethiazide. Five milligrams — no, two point five milligrams. One every morning, for the blood pressure. Been years.
[SEG0026] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And he does take that one. Every morning. I see him do it.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): And alcohol? I'm not going to lecture you, I just need the picture.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Weekends. A couple of beers. Saturday, sometimes the Sunday as well. Not in the week.
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Both days, and it's more than a couple. He's right about the weeknights, though.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever with this, or do you feel unwell in yourself?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No temperature. I'm right as rain apart from the toe being a nuisance.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anywhere else sore? Another toe, an ankle, a knee?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Just this one. Nowhere else.

[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's have a look. Shoe and sock off for me. The right big toe joint is swollen, red and warm, and it's very tender as soon as I press it. The skin's intact, and the rest of the foot looks normal.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Very tender is pushing it. A bit sensitive, that's all.

[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're welcome to play it down. My working impression is a gout flare in that joint. The episode a year back was probably the same thing. I wouldn't call it confirmed, not before a blood test.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Gout? That's old men and port, isn't it. Feels like a lot of drama for one toe.

[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Weekend beer can set it off, and a water tablet like yours can push the uric acid up. I'll request a blood test for uric acid, and kidney function on the same sample, seeing as you're on the bendroflumethiazide.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): It'll have gone before you get the result. Still, if you reckon it's worth it.

[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): For the pain I'm prescribing colchicine. I nearly wrote one milligram twice a day, but don't take that — it's five hundred micrograms twice a day, for five days. Stop if you get diarrhoea.
[SEG0041] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And if that doesn't agree with him?

[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the colchicine doesn't suit him and he has to stop, naproxen five hundred milligrams twice a day with food instead, not both together. Keep the foot up, ease off the beer this weekend, and carry on with the blood pressure tablet as usual.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in two weeks so we can go through that blood result.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): And if the toe gets worse, or you feel feverish before then, come back sooner rather than waiting.

spec.situation: Man with a very painful swollen big toe since last night; drinks beer at weekends, takes a water tablet; had the same 'a year back'; says no injury then recalls kicking a chair; colchicine or NSAID plan; blood uric acid test.
features: self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

omissions.text: Pain severity was described by the patient as 'three out of ten'.

The patient initially denied injury to the toe, then corrected this to having kicked a dining chair the night before; there was uncertainty about timing, ending with the kick happening first and swelling starting later in bed.
Negative finding asked and answered: no other toe, ankle, or knee was sore; only this toe was affected.
The doctor explicitly instructed not to take colchicine at the nearly-written incorrect dose of 1 mg twice a day; the correct dose is 500 micrograms twice a day.
Naproxen was to be taken instead of colchicine 'not both together'.
The planned follow-up in two weeks was specifically to review the blood test result.
